The NBIC R-stamp: the repair organisation side of the question

Short answer: The R endorsement is a qualification held by an inspector. The R-stamp is something different: the National Board "R" Certificate of Authorization, held by a repair organisation. It authorises the holder to repair and alter boilers, pressure vessels and other pressure-retaining items under the National Board Inspection Code (NBIC). An R-stamp holder needs an inspection agreement with an Authorized Inspection Agency, and that agency's R-endorsed inspector inspects the work. If your RFP covers repairs, specify all three: the repair organisation, its AIA and the owner's API 510 inspector.

The National Board governs R-stamp accreditation through NB-415, Accreditation of Repair Organizations. On its R-stamp page, the National Board lists what a new applicant needs:

  • an inspection agreement with an Authorized Inspection Agency;
  • a written quality system that meets the current NBIC and NB-415;
  • current NBIC editions;
  • the construction codes relevant to the intended scope of work;
  • an application on the National Board's form.

The quality system is reviewed onsite before the certificate is issued. That review can be done jointly with an ASME review or on its own. Certificates run for a three-year period.

API 510 recognises the R-stamp directly. In its definitions, API 510 lists the organisations that qualify as a repair organisation:

  • the holder of a valid ASME Certificate of Authorization;
  • the holder of another recognised construction-code certificate;
  • the holder of a valid National Board R-stamp for pressure vessel repair;
  • the holder of a VR-stamp for repair and servicing of relief valves.

Check the definitions section of your current edition for the full list. The list also allows for owner-user organisations and contractors acceptable to the owner, where the jurisdiction permits. The practical result is that many US sites running a pure API 510 programme still have the National Board system on site whenever a contractor holding an R-stamp makes a pressure-boundary weld repair.

The NBIC in one paragraph

NB-23, the National Board Inspection Code, is published in four parts:

  • Part 1, Installation: requirements for installing pressure-retaining items so they function properly.
  • Part 2, Inspection: how to perform and document in-service inspections, including NDE, failure mechanisms and assessment approaches.
  • Part 3, Repairs and Alterations: how to perform, verify and document repairs and alterations regardless of the original construction code.
  • Part 4, Pressure Relief Devices: installation, inspection and repair of relief devices.

The 2025 Edition is current. Many jurisdictions adopt the NBIC by reference for in-service equipment, which is why an inspector working for a jurisdiction or an AIA thinks in NBIC terms while an owner's inspector thinks in API 510 terms. Part 3 is where R-stamp work lives. API 510's own repair and alteration rules are where the owner's inspector authorises and accepts that same work. Our NBIC NB-23 summary covers the structure in more detail.

Who certifies pressure vessel inspectors in the US: the whole map

A related question comes up often: who actually certifies pressure vessel inspectors in the United States, and how do API, the National Board and ASME each fit? Four bodies share the job, and none of them covers it all:

BodyWhat it does for inspectionWhat it does not do
API (Individual Certification Programs)Certifies individuals in its in-service codes (API 510, 570, 653) and related programmes. Publishes API 510 itself.Does not give jurisdictional authority or accredit organisations to inspect for a state.
National BoardCommissions inspectors (IS, AI) and endorsements (R, B, O, nuclear). Accredits AIAs, owner-user inspection organisations and repair organisations (R, VR, NR). Publishes the NBIC.Does not certify anyone to run an owner's API 510 programme.
ASMEWrites the Boiler and Pressure Vessel Code and accredits manufacturers to stamp new equipment. Code inspections during construction are done by AI-commissioned inspectors.Does not certify in-service inspectors.
States, cities and provincesDecide by law which equipment needs certificate inspections, which credentials they accept, and whether they issue their own commissions.Rules differ by jurisdiction and many leave some vessel categories unregulated.

In most US refineries, chemical plants and midstream sites, the result is a layered system. API 510 inspectors run the owner's programme. Commissioned inspectors from an insurer's AIA, the jurisdiction or the owner's accredited organisation do whatever certificate inspections the jurisdiction requires. R-endorsed inspectors accept NBIC repairs. AI-commissioned inspectors appear only when new equipment is built or stamped.

The authorized inspection agency as API 510 defines it

API 510's definition of an authorized inspection agency is broader than the National Board's AIA accreditation, and RFP writers sometimes confuse the two. API 510 recognises four types:

  • the inspection organisation of the jurisdiction;
  • the inspection organisation of an insurer licensed or registered to write pressure vessel insurance;
  • an owner-operator's inspection organisation, for its own equipment and not for vessels held for sale or resale;
  • an independent organisation or individual under contract to and directed by the owner-operator, and recognised or not prohibited by the jurisdiction.

The fourth type is why independent API 510 contractors exist. The contractor works under the owner's direction and inside the owner's programme. It does not need National Board accreditation to do API 510 work, but it cannot hold National Board commissions unless it is itself an accredited AIA.

The phrase "Authorized Inspection Agency" therefore means different things in different documents. In an API 510 context it can be your own inspection department. In a National Board context it means an organisation accredited by the National Board (in-service AIAs under NB-369), typically a jurisdiction or an insurer. If your RFP uses the term, say which meaning you intend.

Three questions that decide the midstream answer

For a gas plant, compressor station, fractionator or terminal, work through these in order before writing the personnel clause.

1. Does the state regulate unfired pressure vessels at this location? State boiler and pressure vessel laws differ widely. Some require periodic certificate inspections of unfired vessels. Some regulate boilers only. Many exempt certain categories, such as some oil and gas production equipment, or vessels below set size and pressure thresholds. Where certificate inspections are required, the inspector must meet that jurisdiction's credential rules, which usually means a National Board commission and sometimes a state commission. Confirm with the state's boiler and pressure vessel office for each site. A multi-state operator may get a different answer in every state.

2. Is the process covered by OSHA PSM or EPA RMP? OSHA's process safety management standard, 29 CFR 1910.119(j), requires a written mechanical integrity programme. Inspection and testing must follow recognized and generally accepted good engineering practices, at frequencies consistent with good engineering practice and manufacturers' recommendations. For in-service pressure vessels, API 510 is the practice most US owners adopt. That obligation sits on top of any state certificate inspection and is not replaced by it.

3. Is the vessel plant equipment or part of a regulated pipeline facility? Equipment within PHMSA-regulated pipeline facilities under 49 CFR Part 192 or 195 brings pipeline rules, including operator qualification and integrity management requirements. The plant-to-pipeline boundary affects which inspection code and which personnel rules apply. Settle it vessel by vessel, not site by site.

What the NDE contractor should deliver to both inspectors

Neither an API 510 inspector nor a commissioned inspector normally performs the ultrasonic, radiographic or magnetic particle examinations themselves. Both rely on qualified NDE personnel and review the results. Write the NDE scope so either inspector can use the same package:

  • Thickness data by CML, with the location reference, previous reading and date, so the API 510 inspector can calculate corrosion rates and remaining life directly.
  • Grid or area scans (corrosion mapping) wherever spot readings show localised loss, so minimum thickness is located rather than estimated.
  • Repair-weld examination records: MT or PT after excavation and after welding, and UT or RT of the completed repair, each stating the procedure, acceptance criteria and examiner certification level.
  • Procedures approved by an ASNT NDT Level III for each method, and examiner certifications under the contractor's written practice to SNT-TC-1A or CP-189.
  • Clear separation of data from decisions. The NDE report records what was found. Intervals, repair acceptance and return to service belong to the inspector of record.

Our pages on CML thickness surveys and corrosion mapping show the typical data formats.

Specification mistakes we see in midstream RFPs

  • "API 510 or National Board commissioned" written as alternatives. This lets a bidder meet a jurisdictional requirement with the wrong credential, or a programme requirement with someone who has never run an API 510 programme.
  • Naming the R endorsement but not the repair organisation. The R-endorsed inspector works through the R-stamp holder's AIA. Specify the repair organisation's R Certificate of Authorization, not only the inspector.
  • Asking for an "ASME inspector" for in-service work. The AI commission is for construction. For operating equipment you almost always want IS, with R where repairs are in scope.
  • Ignoring state reciprocity. NB-263 notes that many jurisdictions add their own requirements before a commissioned inspector may work there.
  • Leaving NDE qualification unspecified. An API 510 certificate tests SE-797 thickness measurement, not weld UT. Name the NDE qualification separately.
  • Handing programme decisions to the NDE contractor. Interval setting and repair acceptance stay with the owner's inspector.

When one person can fill both roles

Many experienced inspectors hold both credentials: API 510 certification and a National Board Inservice commission, often with the R endorsement. NB-263 even counts API 510 or API 570 certification towards the education credit points for a commission. That is useful, but it does not merge the two roles. A dual-credentialed inspector working for an insurer's AIA can carry out the state certificate inspection under the commission. Whether the same person can also act as the owner's API 510 inspector depends on who directs the work and on the independence rules in NB-263's code of ethics, which restrict commissioned inspectors from inspecting items their employer owns or maintains, except inside an accredited owner-user inspection organisation. If you want one person on both lines, name both credentials and both roles in the contract. Then confirm with the AIA, and with the jurisdiction where needed, that the arrangement is acceptable. Also plan around renewal dates. API certificates run on three-year cycles from the holder's own date. Every National Board commission expires on December 31.

Canada: provincial authority replaces the state and National Board layer

In Canada, pressure equipment is regulated by each province or territory, generally building on CSA B51. In Alberta, ABSA's AB-506 sets inspection and servicing requirements for in-service pressure equipment. AB-512 covers owner-user pressure equipment integrity management systems. AB-526 sets the requirements for In-service Pressure Equipment Inspector certification, and ABSA's published route recognises passing the National Board inservice commission exam or the API 510 exam as part of the evidence. Check the current AB-526. Ontario's TSSA and other provincial authorities have their own regimes. For a Canadian facility, the provincial certificate of competency or authorisation is what lets an inspector act. API 510 and National Board credentials support that, but they do not replace it.

How Atlantis fits on an R-stamp or API 510 job

Atlantis NDT is not an Authorized Inspection Agency, does not hold commissioned inspectors and does not act as inspector of record. We perform the NDE both systems rely on. ASNT-certified technicians, working under ASNT Level III oversight, carry out UT thickness and CML surveys, corrosion mapping, PAUT and TOFD on welds, MT and PT on repair excavations and finished welds, radiography with crews licensed where the work is, and visual examination. Results go to your API 510 inspector and to the R-endorsed inspector where one is involved. See pressure vessel inspection services. More questions

What is the NBIC R-stamp?

It is the National Board "R" Certificate of Authorization for organisations that repair or alter boilers, pressure vessels and other pressure-retaining items under the NBIC. NB-415 governs it, it requires an AIA inspection agreement and a reviewed quality system, and it runs for three years.

What is the difference between the R-stamp and the R endorsement?

The R-stamp is held by the repair organisation. The R endorsement is held by the inspector who inspects that organisation's repairs and alterations.

What does "National Board R" mean on a vessel?

It shows that a repair or alteration was made by an R Certificate holder and documented under the NBIC, with inspection by an R-endorsed inspector.

What is NBIC NB-23?

NB-23 is the National Board Inspection Code. It is published in four parts: Installation, Inspection, Repairs and Alterations, and Pressure Relief Devices.

Do we need an R-stamp contractor if we follow API 510?

API 510 accepts several kinds of repair organisation, of which an R-stamp holder is one. Whether you must use one depends on your jurisdiction and your company standards. Talk to us about repair NDE.
